title: Introduction
text: Introduction horizon-mods-lib is a library of native mods for Horizon , the free, open-source rewrite of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 in Rust. Every mod is its own small project with its own tests, its own release and its own .hnmod file. They are ports: each one re-implements something people already use in Fabric (a FPS readout, a zoom, a key overlay, waypoints) on Horizon's native hook points. What a native mod is A Fabric mod is Java that gets loaded into the JVM. A Horizon native mod is Rust source that horizon-mixins merges into the game's own source before it is compiled. The launcher builds a game for the instance the mod is installed in, so the mod is not a plugin loaded at run time: it is part of the executable you play. That has consequences, and this library is built around them: A mod can only do what the game's source lets it hook. Horizon keeps a short list of stable hook points (see Hook points ); mods written against them build on any Horizon whose hook-point version is new enough. A native mod runs with the player's rights, so the registry reads the source of every native mod before it lists it. These projects are small on purpose: a mod's logic is one runtime.rs file with unit tests, and each hook is a helper of a few lines. Everything is MIT, nothing is minified, and the .hnmod contains exactly the .rs and .toml files you can read in the repository. What is here Mods 9 projects in mods/ , one folder each Catalogue The 186 mods in the Tempest cross-pack matrix and where each stands on Horizon Modules Tempest's own module list, and an overview of the Horizon organisation Credits , Licensing , DMCA Who made what, under which terms, and how to ask for something to come down Where to go next Install a mod if you want to play with one. Build from source if you want to change one. Anatomy of a mod and Hook points if you want to write the next one.

title: Install a mod
text: Install a mod Native mods are built into your game, so installing one means building one. The first build downloads Rust and can take 20 to 30 minutes; later builds are faster ( Horizon's native mods guide has the measured numbers). 1. Get the .hnmod Every mod has a GitHub release named -v with the .hnmod and its SHA-256 next to it. Download both and check the hash: sha256sum -c zoomify_1.0.0.hnmod.sha256 The tag and file name are zoomify-v1.0.0 and zoomify-1.0.0.hnmod ; the hash file names the exact file it covers. 2. Unpack it A .hnmod is a zip: horizon-native.json and mixins/ /… with the sources. Unpack it into its own folder: mkdir zoomify && cd zoomify && unzip ../zoomify-1.0.0.hnmod Read the files first. That is the point of a source-only bundle: runtime.rs is the whole logic, the other .rs files are one hook each. 3. Build it into your game Native mods are experimental in Horizon and the launcher asks you to trust the code. From the command line: horizon-launcher native-build ./zoomify --instance MyInstance --trust-native-code The folder can hold one unpacked bundle or several, so you can build a set of mods into one game. The launcher builds on the Horizon commit the mods name, or on the commit of the version you play when the mods name none. All mods in one build must agree on that commit; mods that use only the hook points (these all do) do not pin one. 4. Switch it on In the game, open Options → Mods . Each mod has a row with its description, a settings page and, where it has keys (the two zoom mods), the keys listed first. Getting it into the launcher's browser The launcher's Mods page lists what is in horizon-rust/horizon-mods , after a maintainer has read the source. These projects are not listed there unless their maintainers submitted them; read that repository's MOD-POLICY.md before doing so.

title: Build from source
text: Build from source You need Rust, Python 3.12+ and Git. The mods' own logic builds and tests with plain cargo ; checking them against Horizon needs Horizon's source and a few system libraries. Test a mod's logic cd mods/zoomify cargo fmt --check cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings cargo test --locked The Cargo library of each project is mixins/ /runtime.rs , the same file that horizon-mixins merges into the game, so what you test is what ships. Apply and type-check on Horizon tools/mods.py is adapted from the registry's own tool ( horizon-rust/horizon-mods , native/tools/native.py , MIT): python3 tools/mods.py list # every project python3 tools/mods.py check zoomify # apply on the pinned Horizon, cargo check the game python3 tools/mods.py check all # every mod together, as a player's set is python3 tools/mods.py package zoomify # target/zoomify-1.0.0.hnmod and its SHA-256 check downloads Horizon's source at the commit in compatibility.json (GitHub's archive, never a checkout), builds horizon-mixins at its pinned commit, applies the mods and runs cargo check on the modded game with warnings denied. On Ubuntu the game's crates need libasound2-dev libudev-dev libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev pkg-config . Pins compatibility.json in each project names the Horizon commit it was tested on and the horizon-mixins commit it was applied with, and "hooks": 1 : the hook-point API version it needs. See Compatibility .

title: Hook points
text: Hook points The hook points are empty functions in Horizon's crates/horizon-client/src/game/native_hooks.rs . The game calls them at fixed places; a native mod hooks them with HEAD injections. They keep their names and signatures from release to release and are only ever added; each addition raises NATIVE_HOOKS_API (3 at the commit these projects were tested on). Hook Called These projects use it for native_frame(elapsed) Once a frame Nothing yet native_tick() Once a tick, in every Game (check native_window() ) info-hud : speed from how far you moved native_world_lifecycle(…) World open, open failed, final close (API 3) Nothing yet native_hud(batch, corners) The HUD, not under F1 Every HUD mod: corners.place a box, draw with native_fill and native_text native_key(key, pressed) A key or mouse button, by vanilla name zoomify , simple-zoom native_wheel(steps, claimed) Wheel steps while playing The zoom mods claim them while zoomed native_command(command, ran) A chat command, before the server sees it /fps , /wp , /hud … native_zoom(zoom) Each frame while playing The zoom mods set factor, smoothing and turn scale native_minimap(minimap) Each frame Nothing here; Horizon ships a minimap native_mods(mods) Options → Mods lists native mods Every mod pushes its row native_settings(mod_id, buttons) A mod's settings page opens Every mod pushes its buttons native_settings_click(mod_id, button) A button was clicked Every mod flips its option native_panel_event(…) The item panel's clicks (API 2) Nothing yet Helpers the game gives a mod native_on , native_playing , native_window , native_corner_shown , native_text_width , native_fill , native_text , native_player (position, yaw, pitch, dimension), native_frame_rate , native_clicks , native_mapping , native_mod_key , native_chat , native_data_dir , native_setting , native_set_setting , and the item and recipe helpers of API 2. What the hook points cannot do yet No inventory, effects, incoming chat, camera, input injection or world data beyond the player's position. That is the reason most of the catalogue is marked needs a hook point : armour and potion HUDs need the inventory and effects, chat mods need incoming chat, Freecam and Freelook need the camera. Raising a hook point is a change to Horizon, not to a mod; the contract is described in docs/native-mods.md and native-hooks.json in the Horizon repository.

title: Anatomy of a mod
text: Anatomy of a mod mods/zoomify/ Cargo.toml the Cargo library: points at runtime.rs Cargo.lock compatibility.json pinned Horizon and horizon-mixins commits, hooks API LICENSE README.md mixins/zoomify/ horizon-mixin.toml module + HEAD injections runtime.rs logic, state and tests (one file) key.rs wheel.rs zoom.rs one helper per hook list.rs settings.rs click.rs the Options > Mods row and page horizon-mixin.toml Declares one module (the file runtime.rs , added to the game's game.rs as game::lib_ ) and one injection per hook: [[module]] id = "runtime" file = "crates/horizon-client/src/game.rs" name = "lib_zoomify" source = "runtime.rs" [[injection]] id = "wheel" kind = "HEAD" target = "horizon_client::game::native_hooks::Game ::native_wheel" helper = "wheel.rs" bindings = [ { name = "game", ty = "&crate::game::Game ", value = "&*self" }, { name = "steps", ty = "f32", value = "steps" }, { name = "claimed", ty = "&mut bool", value = "&mut *claimed" }, ] A HEAD injection runs the helper before the hook point's own body, which is empty. Helper names are prefixed with the mod's id ( zoomify_wheel ) because every mod in a build ends up in the same module. runtime.rs Pure logic: no game types. It holds the mod's state in a thread_local! , reads settings through a closure the helper passes in ( |k| game.native_setting(ID, k) ), and carries its unit tests. That is what makes a native mod testable without the game. The helpers Each helper is a few lines: check game.native_on(ID) , read what it needs from the game, call into runtime.rs , draw or store the result. A mod that is switched off in Options → Mods does nothing until the next build leaves it out, so every helper checks first. compatibility.json and the manifest tools/mods.py package writes horizon-native.json into the .hnmod from compatibility.json : {"schema": 1, "id": "zoomify", "version": "1.0.0", "game": "26.3", "horizon": "ba6344a59cb9e755b730dcf02285fc0d33b97d3c", "mixins": "d9c83d7096b7ea5b83678da2efdfd6161f74997e", "hooks": 1} The launcher validates it ( schema 1 , exact 40-character revisions, hooks not zero) before it builds anything and refuses bundles with links, absolute paths or more than 512 entries.

title: Settings and storage
text: Settings and storage A native mod keeps its settings in files, one file per key, in horizon-mods/.horizon-mod-data/ / next to the game's options. game.native_setting(id, key) reads one (trimmed), game.native_set_setting(id, key, value) writes one. These projects store booleans as true and false ; anything else reads as the option's default. Zoom mods also store level (one of 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16). Waypoints stores every waypoint in one file called waypoints , one tab-separated line each ( name x y z dimension ); a line that does not read is skipped, not fatal. Keys are different: they belong to the game's controls. A mod lists keys in its Options → Mods row ( keys in NativeMod : name, label, default) and reads the player's choice with native_mod_key . Both zoom mods list one key. State that is not a setting (the zoom while it is on, the last position for speed, the tracked waypoint) lives in a thread_local! in runtime.rs and is gone when the game closes.

title: Releases
text: Releases Every project releases itself. Change the mod, and bump version in mods/ /mixins/ /horizon-mixin.toml (and Cargo.toml ). Push to main . .github/workflows/release- .yml calls the shared _release.yml , which runs cargo fmt --check , clippy with warnings denied and cargo test , packages the .hnmod , uploads it as a workflow artifact and, if the tag -v does not exist yet , creates that GitHub release with the .hnmod and a .sha256 file. A push that does not change a mod's folder does not trigger its workflow, and a push that does not change the version releases nothing. To test and package without releasing, run a workflow by hand from the Actions tab and leave publish off. ci.yml runs on every push and pull request: each mod's tests in a matrix, and a job that applies all mods on the pinned Horizon and type-checks the game, so a hook that no longer matches Horizon fails there and not on a player's machine. Versioning Semantic versions, per mod. A change that needs a newer hook-point API also bumps hooks in compatibility.json . A new Horizon commit is tested by changing horizon_revision (in compatibility.json and horizon-mixin.toml ) and letting CI apply the set.

title: Compatibility
text: Compatibility Game Minecraft Java 26.3, as implemented by Horizon Horizon (tested on) ba6344a59cb9e755b730dcf02285fc0d33b97d3c (Nightly 2026-10-30) horizon-mixins d9c83d7096b7ea5b83678da2efdfd6161f74997e (0.6.0, plan schema 6) Hook points hooks: 1 : builds on any Horizon whose NATIVE_HOOKS_API is 1 or later Rust Whatever the launcher brings (it downloads its own toolchain); CI uses stable Because these mods hook only the stable hook points, the Horizon commit is the one they were tested on , not a requirement: the launcher builds them on the commit the other mods in the build pin, else on the commit of the installed version. A hook point that is removed or changed incompatibly would break them, and Horizon's contract is that it does not do that. Native mods are not built for dedicated servers yet; on a server you join, only client-side hooks do anything and the protocol is unchanged. In single player and on a LAN host the mods run in the host's game.

title: Mod catalogue
text: Mod catalogue Every mod in the Tempest project's cross-pack matrix ( docs/MOD-MATRIX.md in pxdns/patcher ): 186 mods , 5 ported · 2 partly ported · 44 needs a hook point · 31 pack or asset · 31 engine or server · 28 library · 45 no 26.3 build. Horizon implements Minecraft 26.3 , so the 26.3 column decides what can be ported at all. A native Horizon mod can only use what Horizon's native hook points expose (frame, tick, HUD, key, wheel, command, zoom, minimap, mods list, settings and the world lifecycle, plus the item panel and recipes), which is why most Fabric mods that rewrite rendering, networking or inventories wait for more hook points. The status below says which case each mod is in; nothing is marked ported unless a project in mods/ builds and passes its tests. Status Status Meaning Ported A project in mods/ implements it for Horizon, independently of the upstream code Partly ported Only the part the hook points allow is in a project Needs a hook point Wanted, but Horizon does not expose what it needs yet Pack or asset Belongs in the registry as a resource, shader or data pack Engine or server Performance or server work that Horizon's own engine replaces Library A helper other Fabric mods load; native mods do not use it No 26.3 build The upstream mod has no build for Horizon's game version Upstream licences are copied from each project's Modrinth page. They are listed for credit and to show that this repository copies no upstream code or art: every port is a clean re-implementation of the behaviour. title: Modules
text: Modules Tempest's modules The Tempest client ( pxdns/patcher ) groups its features into modules. title: DMCA and takedowns
text: DMCA and takedowns This library re-implements the behaviour of other people's mods. If you think a project here copies your work, or that something else in this repository infringes a right you hold, you can have it looked at and, if you are right, removed. How to send a notice Open an issue at pxdns/horizon-mods-lib titled DMCA notice , or, if you prefer not to post publicly, message the repository owner pxdns through their GitHub profile and ask for a private channel. GitHub also takes notices directly under its own DMCA policy , which applies to this repository whatever is done here. A notice should have the elements the law asks for (17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(3)): Your name and a way to contact you. The work you say is infringed, with a link to it. The material here you say infringes, with the file path or URL (a line range helps). A statement that you believe in good faith that the use is not authorised by the owner, its agent or the law. A statement that the information in the notice is accurate and, under penalty of perjury, that you are the owner or authorised to act for the owner. Your physical or electronic signature. What happens next The material is reviewed within a few days. If it is infringing, or if there is real doubt, it is removed from main and from the site, the release asset is deleted, and the project's page says so. Where the complaint is that a port is too close to the original, the fix may be a rewrite rather than a removal; you will be told which. Counter-notice If something was taken down and you believe that was a mistake, send a counter-notice by the same route with your name, contact details, the material removed and where it was, a statement under penalty of perjury that you believe in good faith it was removed by mistake or misidentification, and your consent to the jurisdiction of the federal court for your address (or, outside the US, any judicial district in which GitHub may be found), and your signature. Material may be restored after the period the law allows, unless the sender tells us they have gone to court. Repeat infringers Contributors who repeatedly submit infringing material lose the right to contribute. This page describes how the project handles notices. It is not legal advice.

title: Security
text: Security A native mod is native code with the player's rights. That is true of every native Horizon mod, and the launcher says so in red before it builds one. What this library does about it: Source only. A .hnmod contains .rs , .toml , a LICENSE and horizon-native.json , nothing compiled. You can read all of it, and the launcher checks the bundle without running anything. Small by design. Each mod's logic is one file with unit tests; the helpers are a few lines each. There is no unsafe , no network access, no process spawning and no dependency in any Cargo.toml . The only files a mod touches are its own settings files through native_set_setting . Reproducible. The .hnmod is packaged deterministically (fixed timestamps, sorted entries), so the same commit gives the same SHA-256, which the release publishes beside the file. Pinned. compatibility.json names exact commits of Horizon and horizon-mixins, never a branch or a tag. If you find a vulnerability, open a private security advisory on the repository (Security tab → Report a vulnerability) rather than a public issue.

title: Contributing
text: Contributing Ports are welcome. A good one is small, tested, and honest about what the hook points let it do. Pick a mod that fits the hook points. The catalogue marks what needs a hook point and what does not; if a mod needs one, the useful contribution is a pull request to Horizon that adds the hook point. Copy a project folder under mods/ and rename it ( slug for the folder, snake_case for the id). Keep runtime.rs pure, put the tests in it, keep each helper a few lines. Write it from behaviour. Do not copy or translate upstream code. See Licensing . Run cargo fmt , cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings , cargo test --locked , and python3 tools/mods.py check . Add a release- .yml (copy an existing one and change the slug), a row in docs/credits.md , and an icon in assets/icons/ . Open the pull request. CI applies all mods on the pinned Horizon. Be accurate in README claims: say what the mod does and what it does not, and name the upstream mod and its licence.

title: Home
text: Native mods for Horizon Your favourite mods, rewritten in Rust. Horizon is a rewrite of Minecraft: Java in Rust, and its mods are not plugins: they are source that gets merged into the game and compiled with it. This is a library of them. 9 are done, each one a tiny project with its own tests, its own release and a file you can read in five minutes. See the mods Install one How a Fabric mod becomes Rust 9 mods shipped 48 unit tests across them 0 dependencies in any mod 141 of 186 catalogued mods have a 26.3 build A mod is part of the game, not a guest in it Fabric loads Java into a running JVM. Horizon has no JVM. A native mod is Rust that horizon-mixins merges into Horizon's source before the compiler sees it, and the launcher builds a game for your instance with the mods already inside. Hook Horizon keeps a short list of stable hook points: empty functions the game calls every frame, tick, key press, HUD draw. Merge A horizon-mixin.toml says which hook runs which helper, and adds the mod's runtime.rs to the game as a module. Build The launcher compiles the modded source for your instance. First build 20 to 30 minutes, later ones faster. Play Switch the mod on or off in Options, Mods. It has a settings page and, if it needs one, a key. The 9 mods Each folder in mods/ is a complete project: logic, tests, pins, licence, a release workflow. They are ports, written from how the originals behave and not from their code. FPS Display Frames per second in a corner of the screen, coloured by how smooth they are. fps_display 1.0.0 · 4 tests Sprint Indicator Shows Sprinting, Walking or Sneaking in a corner of the screen while you move. sprint_indicator 1.0.0 · 4 tests Key Overlay Shows W, A, S, D, jump and the mouse buttons on screen and lights the ones you hold. key_overlay 1.0.0 · 5 tests CPS Counter Your clicks per second in a corner of the screen. cps_counter 1.0.0 · 3 tests Info HUD Your speed, the way you face and your dimension in a corner of the screen, in the spirit of MiniHUD's info lines. info_hud 1.0.0 · 6 tests Custom HUD One box with the lines you pick: FPS, coordinates, facing and clicks per second, on the side you choose. custom_hud 1.0.0 · 4 tests Zoomify Hold a key to zoom in, turn the wheel to zoom further, with smooth easing and slower turning. zoomify 1.0.0 · 7 tests Simple Zoom Press a key to zoom in and press it again to zoom out; the wheel changes the zoom meanwhile. simple_zoom 1.0.0 · 7 tests Waypoints Name places with /wp, list them, and track one: its distance and direction show on screen. waypoints 1.0.0 · 8 tests All 186 mods in the catalogue, with where each one stands → What we do not pretend 44 of the 186 catalogued mods are wanted but cannot be written yet, because the hook points do not give a mod an inventory, effects, incoming chat or the camera. Nothing here is marked ported unless a project builds, passes its tests and type-checks against a real Horizon. What Horizon needs to expose How it is kept honest Verified today: all 9 mods apply on Horizon ba6344a with horizon-mixins d9c83d7 and the game type-checks with warnings denied. They are unit-tested, formatted and clippy-clean. They have not been played in a live game by this project's CI, which cannot run a GPU build.

title: Why native mods
text: Why native Mods you can read, test and trust. A plugin system is a promise that code you did not read will behave. Horizon's native mods make a smaller promise and keep it: the bundle is source, and the source is short. There is nothing to load A Fabric mod is a jar the game opens at start-up, patches with bytecode tricks and runs inside the same JVM. Horizon is native Rust, so a mod cannot be loaded that way, and does not need to be. horizon-mixins works on the game's source tree: it parses the Rust, applies the injections a mod declares, and the compiler sees one program. A hook is a function call that was written into the game before it was built. No reflection, no class loader, nothing that decides at run time what runs. The bundle is the source A .hnmod is a zip of .rs and .toml files and a licence. Nothing compiled is in it. The launcher checks it without running anything, refuses links, odd paths and anything beyond the bundle layout, and then builds it for your instance behind a red warning, because native code has the player's rights. Horizon's registry lists a native mod only after a maintainer has read its source. You can do the same in the time it takes to drink a coffee: here, a mod's logic is one file of a few hundred lines at most. Logic that does not need the game to test Each project's Cargo library is its runtime.rs . The game's types never appear in it; the hook helpers read what they need and pass plain values in. That is why a zoom's wheel limits, a waypoint's bearing maths and a speedometer's smoothing have unit tests that run in under a second, and why a bug in them is a failed test instead of a crashed game. Small on purpose There are no dependencies in any of these projects. There is no unsafe , no network access and no process spawning. A mod that is switched off in Options does nothing at all until the next build leaves it out. Settings are one file per key in the mod's own folder. What it costs Build time. Every set of mods is a build of the game: the first one downloads a toolchain and takes 20 to 30 minutes, a rebuild of one changed helper takes a few minutes. Reach. A native mod can only do what a hook point allows. Servers. Native mods are not built for dedicated servers yet; on a server you join, only client-side hooks do anything. Maturity. Native mods are experimental in Horizon. We say so on every page that matters. See how a port goes The hook points

title: From Fabric to Horizon
text: Porting From Fabric to Horizon, one behaviour at a time. The Tempest project has a matrix of 186 Fabric mods across five game versions. This is what happens when you take that list to a game written in Rust. Start with the list Horizon implements Minecraft 26.3, so the first filter is blunt: 45 of the 186 mods have no 26.3 build and are out. Of the remaining 141, most are libraries, performance mods a native engine does not need, or packs. What is left is a short list of mods that are about what you see and press. Ported 5 Partly ported 2 Needs a hook point 44 Pack or asset 31 Engine or server 31 Library 28 No 26.3 build 45 Rule one: copy the behaviour, never the code Upstream mods are LGPL, GPL, MIT, all-rights-reserved. A port that contains none of their code owes them credit and nothing else, and it owes the reader an honest account of what it does. So each port starts from using the original, writing down what it does, and writing Rust. The credits name every original and its licence. Rule two: the logic gets tests Zoomify's wheel clamps between 1.25x and 16x. A test fails if it does not. Waypoints compute a vanilla yaw to a block; one test pins north, south, east and west. The hook helpers cannot be tested without the game, so they are kept to a few lines, and CI type-checks them against the real Horizon. Rule three: say what is missing Xaero's minimap is only partly ported: Horizon ships its own minimap, and there is no map-screen hook, so what is left is the waypoints idea. The catalogue says so. A port, end to end Zoomify holds a key and zooms. On Horizon that is three hooks. The key hook is this much code: // The zoom key went down or up: the player's own choice of key. fn zoomify_key(game: &mut crate::game::Game , key: &str, pressed: bool) { use crate::game::lib_zoomify as m; // Turned off in Options > Mods: nothing until the next build leaves it out. if !game.native_on(m::ID) { return; } if key != game.native_mod_key(m::ID, m::KEY, m::DEFAULT_KEY) { return; } let playing = game.native_playing(); let game = &*game; m::key(playing, pressed, |name| game.native_setting(m::ID, name)); } And the wheel claims its steps while the zoom is on, so the hotbar does not move: // While the zoom is on, the wheel changes it instead of moving the hotbar. fn zoomify_wheel(game: &crate::game::Game , steps: f32, claimed: &mut bool) { use crate::game::lib_zoomify as m; if game.native_on(m::ID) && m::wheel(steps) { *claimed = true; } } Everything else (the levels, the easing flag, the turn scaling, the settings buttons) lives in runtime.rs and has seven tests.

title: Trust
text: Trust Built so that you do not have to take our word. A native mod runs with your rights. Here is everything this library does about that, and what it asks of you. Source, not binaries A .hnmod holds Rust and TOML. Read it before you build it; the launcher validates it without running anything. Pinned and reproducible Exact Horizon and horizon-mixins commits in every project. The package is deterministic: same commit, same SHA-256, published beside the file. Clean-room ports Written from behaviour. No upstream code, art or text, and the credits name every original and its licence. Original icons Each mod's icon is drawn for this library. No upstream logo is bundled or hot-linked. Nothing phones home No network access in any mod, no dependencies, no analytics on this site, no third-party fonts or scripts. A way to say stop If something here is yours and should not be, the DMCA page says how to ask, and what happens next. The honest limits. This is an unofficial project, not endorsed by the Horizon project, Mojang or Microsoft. Native mods are experimental in Horizon. The mods are unit-tested and type-checked against Horizon in CI, and have not been played through a real window by CI. Read the security notes and the disclaimer .

text: Roadmap What is waiting on Horizon, not on us. 44 catalogued mods cannot be written yet. The reason is never effort: it is that a hook point does not exist. Hook points are only ever added, so each one that lands unblocks a group of them. 13 mods Needs a hook point Horizon does not have yet (the current hook points are listed in the docs). Better Statistics Screen, BetterGrassify, Clumps, Item Highlighter, Marlow's Crystal Optimizer, Pearl Optimizer, ScalableLux, [ETF] Entity Texture Features… 13 mods Needs input or camera hooks that Horizon does not expose yet. Combat Hitboxes, Controlling, EntityCrosshair, Freecam, Gamma-Utils-Fabric, InvMove, Mouse Tweaks, SnappyTappy… 10 mods Needs inventory, effect or item data that the hook points do not give a mod yet. AppleSkin, Detail Armor Bar Reconstructed, Durability Tooltip, Pick Up Notifier, Shulker Box Tooltip, potioncounter-fabric, status-effect-bars, statuseffecttimer… 6 mods Needs incoming-chat or screen hooks that Horizon does not expose yet.
